title: Assam Floods Devastate Tea Estates as Army Deploys and Over 1.7 Lakh People Affected
excerpt: Fresh monsoon flooding submerges Upper Assam's tea-growing heartland in Nazira and Sivasagar, with four family members swept away and rail services disrupted across the region.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Over 1.7 lakh people affected by fresh flooding in Upper Assam, with army deployed for rescue.
  • Tea estates in Nazira and Sivasagar, crucial to Assam's $1.5 billion tea industry, are submerged.
  • Four family members swept away in flash floods, raising concerns over rescue response delays.
  • Rail services disrupted across Upper Assam as rivers flow above danger levels amid forecasted heavy rainfall.

  • Fresh flooding in Upper Assam has affected over 1.7 lakh people across multiple districts, with the army deployed for rescue operations
  • Tea estates in Nazira and Sivasagar — the heart of Assam's $1.5 billion tea industry — are submerged under floodwaters
  • Four members of a single family were swept away in flash floods, with villagers alleging delayed rescue response
  • Rail services across the region have been disrupted, and rivers continue to flow above danger levels

A fresh wave of monsoon flooding has engulfed Upper Assam, submerging tea estates across Nazira and Sivasagar and forcing the Indian Army to deploy rescue columns as the situation deteriorates rapidly. More than 1.7 lakh people have been affected across multiple districts, according to the Assam State Disaster Management Authority.

The Tea Association of India has described the situation as "deeply concerning," with several estates in the region's prime tea-growing belt left underwater. Assam produces roughly 52% of India's tea and accounts for a significant share of the global supply — disruptions to the estates during peak plucking season could ripple through markets worldwide.

Tragedy Strikes Families

In one of the most devastating incidents, four members of a single family were swept away by flash floods in the region. Villagers have alleged a delay in the rescue response, adding to growing criticism of disaster preparedness in the state.

Rail services across Upper Assam have been disrupted as tracks remain submerged, cutting off communities from major urban centers. The Brahmaputra River and several tributaries continue to flow above danger levels, with the India Meteorological Department forecasting more heavy rainfall in the coming days.

Army-Led Rescue Operations

The Indian Army has deployed multiple flood relief columns across the affected districts, working alongside the National Disaster Response Force and state teams. Rescue operations using boats and helicopters are underway to evacuate stranded residents from rooftops and elevated areas.

Impact on Tea Estates

Hundreds of villages remain inundated, with thousands of hectares of cropland — including paddy fields and tea gardens — submerged. Local officials report that roads, bridges, and embankments have suffered significant damage.

Economic Impact

The timing of the floods is particularly damaging for the tea industry. The second flush season — which produces the prized muscatel teas most valued in international markets — is in full swing. Extended waterlogging can damage tea bushes and reduce yields for months, compounding losses from earlier flood waves that hit the state in June.

For Assam's 800,000 tea workers and their families, the floods threaten both immediate safety and long-term livelihoods in an industry that forms the backbone of the region's economy.

What's Next

Assam Chief Minister Himanta Biswa Sarma has said the state government is working on a comprehensive rehabilitation program for those affected. The military remains on standby for further deployments as meteorological agencies warn that water levels in the Brahmaputra are expected to remain elevated through the end of the week.
